We don't float, but we do find the 'calmness and serenity' promised on Page 84. The Promises come true when we stop rushing and let God do the heavy lifting.
6-10.discussion: Where in your life today are you trying to force a result instead of trusting your Higher Power's timing?

6-11.thought: Family obligations take on new meaning in recovery. The Big Book reminds us that our first duty is to maintain our own sobriety, for without that we are useless to anyone. But it also warns against using the program as an escape from family responsibilities. On page 127, it says: 'We realize that we have been placed on earth to be of maximum service to God and the people about us.' This includes our families. We're not to neglect them, nor to smother them. Page 130 offers wisdom: 'It is possible to have too much of a good thing.' The key is balance—showing up for our families without letting their problems lure us back to drink. The Promises on page 84 assure us that as we work the Steps, we will know a new freedom and happiness that extends to our home life.
6-11.discussion: How have your family obligations changed since you got sober, and where do you draw the line between helping and over-involvement?

6-12.thought: True partnerships in recovery are not about getting someone to do what you want, but about walking alongside them with humility and love. The Big Book says in Chapter 7, 'We are not to be the arbiter of his destiny, but we are to be the agent of his liberation' [Page 90]. That’s the heart of partnership—you don’t fix people, you carry the message and let them find their own path. And in Chapter 9, we learn that partnership with family means making amends and rebuilding trust, not bossing or controlling [Page 130]. Even our partnership with a Higher Power is a true one: we do the footwork, God provides the grace. The Promises assure us that 'we will intuitively know how to handle situations which used to baffle us' [Page 84]—that’s partnership in action, when we stop trying to run the show and start cooperating with life.
6-12.discussion: Think of a relationship in your life—with a sponsor, a spouse, a friend—where you tend to take charge or control. How could you shift to a true partnership today, letting go of the outcome and simply being present?

6-13.thought: Living our amends means more than a one-time apology — it's a way of life. The Big Book makes clear that 'putting our feet on the path' of Step 9 transforms us: 'We have ceased fighting anything or anyone — even alcohol' [Page 84]. Amends are made 'except when to do so would injure them or others' [Page 76], but the real work is in the living. We become 'painstaking' about adjusting our relationships [Page 83], and the Promises unfold as we practice these principles in all our affairs. That's how amends become living — not a list checked off, but a daily attitude of honesty and humility.
6-13.discussion: Think of a relationship where you've made amends but still feel uneasy. What small, consistent action could you take today to truly live that amend?

6-14.thought: When the going gets rough, we often feel we're back at square one. But the Big Book reminds us that rough patches are exactly when our program works best. On page 83, we read the Promises: 'We will not regret the past nor wish to shut the door on it.' That means even the hard moments are part of our recovery—they teach us humility and dependence on a Power greater than ourselves. And on page 85, it says we are given a daily reprieve contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition. So rough times aren't a sign we've failed; they're an invitation to double down on the Steps, especially Step Eleven — prayer and meditation — which is discussed on pages 86-87. When I'm struggling, I go back to page 63's Third Step Prayer and remember that my job is to trust, not to manage. The Promises will come true, but not on my timeline.
6-14.discussion: When you hit a rough patch in recovery, what's your first move: your sponsor, your Higher Power, or your own best thinking?

6-15.thought: That's a beautiful theme, and one that speaks directly to the heart of Step Two. The Big Book makes it clear that a 'Higher Power' doesn't have to be a traditional God. On page 46, it says, 'When we saw the love and tolerance of the group, we began to admit that a power greater than ourselves could restore us to sanity.' For many newcomers, that love and tolerance is the first evidence of a power beyond their own will. AA itself—the fellowship, the meetings, the collective wisdom—can absolutely serve as your Higher Power. The book even encourages this when it says, 'We found that great reality deep down within us. In the last analysis it is only there that He may be found' (page 55). That reality can be the group conscience, the principles, and the experience of other alcoholics. So if the word 'God' is a roadblock, let AA be your Higher Power—it works just as well.
6-15.book_ref: Chapter 4: We Agnostics, pages 44-57 (especially pages 46 and 55)
6-15.discussion: What is one way you can practice relying on the AA group as a power greater than yourself today, rather than on your own willpower?

6-16.thought: Open-mindedness is the gateway to recovery. In We Agnostics, the Big Book reminds us that 'we had to stop doubting the power of God' and instead become 'willing to believe' [Page 47]. This isn't blind faith—it's a humble willingness to consider that our old ways of thinking have failed us. The book urges us to 'lay aside prejudice and express even a willingness to believe in a Power greater than ourselves' [Page 47]. That simple act of keeping an open mind is often the first crack in the wall of our self-will. Later, on [Page 568], the spiritual experience appendix underscores that a 'complete psychic change' is possible when we are 'open-minded and willing to try something new.' Open-mindedness isn't about having all the answers—it's about being teachable, letting go of the notion that we know best, and allowing a new solution to take root.
6-16.discussion: What is one belief or attitude about yourself, others, or God that you are being called to hold more lightly today?

6-17.thought: Deep down within us, recovery uncovers a spiritual awakening that was always there. The Big Book tells us that a spiritual experience 'means the personality change sufficient to bring about recovery from alcoholism' [567]. This isn't something we manufacture—it's a gift that emerges as we work the Steps. We find that the obsession with drinking is removed, and deep down, a new freedom and happiness appear [84]. This inner change is described as being 'relieved of the bondage of self' [63], allowing us to connect with a Power greater than ourselves and with others. The theme reminds us that transformation isn't external; it's the quiet, deep work of the soul.
6-17.book_ref: Appendix II, pages 567-568; Chapter 6, pages 83-85; Chapter 5, page 63
6-17.discussion: What core belief about yourself has changed deep down since you started working the Steps?

6-18.thought: Freedom in AA isn't just about putting down the drink—it's about being released from the bondage of self. The Big Book promises that we will "know a new freedom and a new happiness" [Page 83] as we work the Steps. That freedom comes from honesty, openness, and willingness to let go of our old ways. We are no longer slaves to alcohol or to our own selfishness. This fellowship offers a safe place where we can practice this freedom, sharing our experience without judgment. As it says, "We are not fighting it, neither are we avoiding temptation" [Page 85]. We are simply free because we have found a Power greater than ourselves.
6-18.discussion: In what area of your life today can you experience a little more freedom by letting go of control or fear?

6-19.thought: Ah, regeneration—a word that speaks to the very heart of our recovery! The Big Book tells us that the alcoholic who has recovered "has had a profound and vital psychic change" [Page xxix]. This isn't just a tweak or a touch-up; it's a complete rebirth of the spirit. In Chapter 5, we read that we become "willing to believe in a Power greater than ourselves" [Page 46], and this willingness opens the door to a whole new way of living. The Promises in Chapter 6 paint a vivid picture of this regeneration: "We will not regret the past nor wish to shut the door on it" [Page 83]. That's not merely behavior change—that's a fundamental transformation of our entire outlook. Regeneration in AA means the old, selfish, driven drinker dies, and a new, grateful, service-minded person emerges [Page 84]. It's not just stopping drinking; it's being remade.
6-19.book_ref: Doctor's Opinion, pages xxix-xxx, and Chapter 6, pages 83-85
6-19.discussion: In what specific ways have you experienced a 'psychic change'—a shift in your thinking and feeling—that goes beyond just not drinking?

6-20.thought: Fear is the great enemy of our sobriety — it blocks us from the very spiritual experience that sets us free. The Big Book teaches us to fearlessly face our fears, listing them on paper in our inventory [Page 67-68] and then asking God to remove them. In the Seventh Step Prayer we say, 'Remove my fear' [Page 76], because we cannot do it alone. When we are released from fear, we find a new freedom and happiness — the Promises tell us fear leaves us and we intuitively know how to handle situations that used to baffle us [Page 84]. This release isn't a one-time event; it's a daily reprieve dependent on our spiritual condition [Page 85]. Keep coming back, keep working the Steps, and fear loses its grip.
6-20.book_ref: Chapter 5: How It Works, pages 67-68; Chapter 6: Into Action, pages 76, 84-85
6-20.discussion: What is one specific fear you can write down today and ask your Higher Power to remove from your life?

6-21.thought: Fear and faith are two sides of the same coin in recovery. The Big Book teaches us that fear is the chief activator of our defects — it's the root of resentment, selfishness, and dishonesty. On [Page 68], we're told to list our fears and ask why we have them, because fear blocks us from God's will. But faith is the antidote. On [Page 85], it says, 'We are not cured of alcoholism. What we really have is a daily reprieve contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition.' That maintenance is faith in action — trusting a Power greater than ourselves to handle what we can't. When fear whispers, 'You're not going to make it,' faith replies, 'I don't have to make it on my own.' So for someone in recovery, this theme means recognizing fear as a signal to double down on spiritual practices: prayer, meditation, and step work. The more we lean into faith, the less room fear has to run the show.
6-21.discussion: What is one specific fear that you've been holding onto, and how could you turn it over to your Higher Power today?

6-22.thought: Ah, 'Today, I'm Free.' That's the heart of it, isn't it? The Big Book promises that we will 'know a new freedom and a new happiness' [Page 83]. For someone in recovery, this isn't just freedom from alcohol — it's freedom from the obsession that once drove us. On page 84, it says, 'We will not regret the past nor wish to shut the door on it.' That's real freedom: no longer a slave to our past mistakes, our resentments, or the compulsion to drink. We wake up each morning knowing we have a choice, and that choice is to live a life of purpose and connection. The freedom comes from working the Steps, especially Step 9 — making amends — which 'clears away the wreckage of the past' [Page 82]. And it's maintained through Step 12, carrying the message to others, which keeps us sober and reminds us just how precious this freedom is. Today, you're free. Don't waste it.
6-22.discussion: Think of one area of your life today — a resentment, a fear, or a relationship — where you feel you might still be trapped. What would a 'free' version of that look like, and what one action could you take today to move closer to that freedom?

6-23.thought: Trusting others is at the heart of the recovery journey. In Chapter 6, we read that when we made a searching and fearless moral inventory, we then "admitted to God, to ourselves, and to another human being the exact nature of our wrongs." [Page 72] This fifth step requires a deep trust in another person—someone who will listen without judgment. Many of us struggled with trust because we had been dishonest or betrayed, but the Big Book promises that as we work the steps, this fear begins to lift. On page 83, we find the promise that "we will intuitively know how to handle situations which used to baffle us"—and part of that intuition is learning to trust the right people. Trusting others is not blind faith; it's a spiritual experiment. We start by trusting God, then a sponsor, then the fellowship, and gradually our capacity for trust grows. The book reminds us that "we have to depend upon the help and guidance of a Higher Power and the fellowship of A.A." [Page 85] Without trust, we remain isolated and powerless. With it, we find a new freedom and a new sense of belonging.
6-23.discussion: What is one small step you can take this week to practice trusting another person in your recovery—whether it's sharing something honest at a meeting or asking for help on a problem?

6-24.thought: The phrase 'A Spiritual Kindergarten' captures a beautiful truth about our program: we are all beginners here. The Big Book doesn't use that exact phrase, but it certainly teaches that we start simple. On page 85, it says we are given a 'daily reprieve' contingent on our spiritual condition. That's kindergarten-level truth—we don't master it, we practice it one day at a time. Just as a child learns the alphabet before reading, we learn to rely on a Power greater than ourselves before we can carry the message. The Promises on pages 83-84 aren't for experts; they're for any alcoholic who honestly works the Steps. So today, embrace your kindergarten status—be teachable, stay humble, and keep coming back. That's where the real growth happens [Page 85, Page 83-84].
6-24.discussion: What is one 'kindergarten-level' spiritual practice you can commit to today to strengthen your daily reprieve?

6-25.thought: You see, the 'two-way street' is at the very heart of our recovery. We don't get sober by keeping sobriety to ourselves—we keep it by giving it away. Just as we once were carried by the strength of others, we now become the hands that lift the next suffering alcoholic. The Big Book puts it plainly: 'Practical experience shows that nothing will so much insure immunity from drinking as intensive work with other alcoholics.' [Page 89, Chapter 7] That's the two-way street—our own sobriety is sustained precisely when we turn around and help the next person. And in doing so, we receive the very promises we clung to: 'We will suddenly realize that God is doing for us what we could not do for ourselves.' [Page 83] It's not a one-way charity; it's a mutual exchange, a living cycle where giving and receiving are one.
6-25.discussion: Think of a time when helping another alcoholic—just a kind word or sharing your story—strengthened your own sobriety. What did you receive in that giving?

6-26.theme: A GIFT THAT GROWS WITH TIME
6-26.thought: The gift of recovery isn't a one-time event—it deepens and expands the longer we live it. The Big Book Promises say we will 'not regret the past nor wish to shut the door on it' [Page 83], and that our whole attitude and outlook on life changes. This is the gift growing: the more we practice the principles in all our affairs, the more peace, usefulness, and joy we receive. Page 85 reminds us that we are only given a daily reprieve, contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition. So the gift isn't static; it requires ongoing action—prayer, inventory, helping others—and it rewards us with ever-deepening serenity and freedom. Each day we stay sober and work the program, the gift becomes richer. That's why it grows with time.
6-26.discussion: Think of your first days of sobriety: what has the gift of recovery given you now that you didn't have in the beginning? How has it changed, and what helped it grow?

6-27.thought: To conform to the A.A. way is not to lose your individuality, but to surrender your old ideas that kept you drinking. As the Big Book says, 'The first requirement is that we be convinced that any life run on self-will can hardly be a success' [Page 62]. This means we stop fighting, we admit we don't know how to live on our own, and we adopt the simple, proven pattern of recovery that millions have walked before us. It's like learning to dance to a new song—awkward at first, but liberating once you let the music lead. The Promises on page 84 assure us that 'We will intuitively know how to handle situations which used to baffle us.' That's the reward of conforming: not rigid rules, but freedom from self-will.
6-27.discussion: What is one old idea you had to let go of in order to fully embrace the program as it is, not as you wish it were?

6-28.thought: The determination of our founders is the bedrock upon which our fellowship stands. Bill Wilson and Dr. Bob, along with the early members, faced countless failures and disappointments, yet they never gave up. In Bill's Story, he describes his own desperate journey [Page 1-16] and how he found hope through carrying the message to others. That same dogged persistence is what built AA. In Chapter 7, we read: 'Practical experience shows that nothing will so much insure immunity from drinking as intensive work with other alcoholics' [Page 89]. The founders understood that their own sobriety depended on passing it on, so they kept at it, one drunk at a time. Their determination wasn't just for themselves—it was a legacy of love for every alcoholic who would come after. For us today, that same spirit means we don't quit when the road gets rough. We keep showing up, keep sharing, keep loving. That's how we honor their determination.
6-28.discussion: What is one area in your recovery today where you need to adopt the founders' determination—staying the course even when results aren't immediate?

6-29.thought: The rippling effect of recovery is one of the most beautiful promises of the program. When one alcoholic gets sober, that change doesn't stay contained — it flows outward. The Big Book describes this in Chapter 7: 'Practical experience shows that nothing will so much insure immunity from drinking as intensive work with other alcoholics.' [Page 89] Your sobriety becomes a stone thrown into still water, sending waves to your family, your friends, and eventually to still-suffering alcoholics you haven't even met. The promises in Chapter 6 tell us 'we will be amazed before we are half way through' at how our lives change [Page 83], and that 'we will know a new freedom and a new happiness' [Page 83] — but this ripple doesn't stop with us. As we stay sober, we become channels of hope. The drunk who sees you living sober may be the next ripple. Your sponsor, the sponsee, the newcomer at their first meeting — each one carries the wave forward. It's not about being perfect; it's about being willing to pass on what was freely given.
6-29.book_ref: Chapter 7, pages 89-103 (Working With Others); Chapter 6, pages 83-84 (The Promises)
6-29.discussion: Think of the ripple effect in your own life: Who was the person whose recovery first touched you? How has your sobriety already sent out waves to others — maybe in ways you didn't even notice at first?

6-30.thought: Ah, my friend, this theme cuts to the heart of our program. You see, sacrifice isn't about deprivation—it's about letting go of the old, self-centered life that kept us drunk. On page 62, it says, 'Half measures availed us nothing. We stood at the turning point. We asked His protection and care with complete abandon.' That surrender, that sacrifice of our ego, is what opens the door to unity. When we stop trying to run the show alone and join with others in the fellowship, we find we're no longer isolated. And from that unity comes survival—not just staying sober, but truly living. Page 84 promises us: 'We will not regret the past nor wish to shut the door on it.' That’s the survival of a new life. So sacrifice isn't loss; it's the very thing that bonds us together and keeps us alive.
6-30.discussion: What is one small thing you could sacrifice today—a resentment, a fear, or a need to be right—that might bring you closer to the unity of the group and strengthen your recovery?

7-1.thought: In recovery, the phrase 'the best for today' reminds us that we don't need to figure out our whole lives at once. The Big Book says we have a 'daily reprieve' contingent on our spiritual condition [85]. That means we only need to stay sober and do the next right thing for today. Yesterday's mistakes are off our shoulders; tomorrow's worries aren't here yet. As it says on page 83, 'We will see that our new attitude toward liquor has been given us without any thought or effort on our part. It comes! That is the miracle of it.' We simply show up today, work the program, and trust that God will do for us what we cannot do for ourselves. The best for today is letting go of the illusion of control and focusing on this one day's journey.
7-1.discussion: What does 'the best for today' look like in your life right now? How can you set aside past regrets and future fears to fully embrace this 24 hours?

7-2.thought: True sobriety isn't just about putting down the bottle — that's only the beginning. The heart of it is a spiritual awakening that transforms how we live. As the Big Book says, 'We have not only stopped drinking, but we have learned to live in the world with peace and serenity' [Page 83]. This happens when we work the Steps and discover a Power greater than ourselves. The Promises tell us we will 'know a new freedom and a new happiness' [Page 83] — that's the heart: freedom from the obsession to drink and freedom to love and serve others. Real sobriety is a daily reprieve contingent on our spiritual condition [Page 85], not a one-time fix. It's about carrying this message to still-suffering alcoholics and living the principles in all our affairs.
7-2.book_ref: Chapter 6, pages 83-85; Chapter 7, pages 89-103; Appendix II, pages 567-568
7-2.discussion: What does 'a new freedom and a new happiness' look like in your life today — are you living from that heart of true sobriety, or just going through the motions?

7-3.thought: In the Big Book, experience isn't just a teacher—it's the only way the message truly comes alive. On page 89, it says, 'The practical experience of the earlier ones proved to be the sound foundation upon which this society has been built.' We don't just read about sobriety; we live it, one day at a time, and then share what we've actually been through. That's why the Promises on pages 83-84 aren't theoretical—they're the fruit of real experience with the Steps. As we work with others, our own experience becomes their best teacher too [Page 89]. It's the difference between knowing the path and walking it.
7-3.discussion: What experience from your recovery has taught you something that no amount of reading or listening could?

7-4.thought: In AA, we often find that faith doesn't come from a dramatic conversion, but grows naturally as we work the Steps. The Big Book says in We Agnostics, 'When we saw others solve their problems by a simple reliance upon the Spirit of the Universe, we had to stop doubting the power of God' [Page 52]. That's the heart of natural faith—it's built on evidence, not blind belief. As we watch others recover and begin to experience relief ourselves, faith becomes less a struggle and more a quiet certainty. By Step 3, we're ready to turn our will and life over to God as we understand Him—not because we've forced ourselves, but because we've seen it work [Page 63]. This natural faith continues to deepen as we practice the remaining Steps, especially through prayer and meditation. It's a gift that unfolds effortlessly when we stay open and honest.
7-4.discussion: What experience in your recovery has made faith feel more natural and less like a struggle?

7-5.thought: A new direction is at the heart of our recovery. The Big Book tells us 'we are going to know a new freedom and a new happiness' [Page 83] when we stop fighting everything and instead let a Higher Power guide our lives. This isn't about just stopping drinking—it's about a complete change in how we think and act. On page 63, the Third Step Prayer asks for God's direction, saying 'I pray that you now remove from me every single defect of character which stands in the way of my usefulness to you and my fellows.' That's the new direction: away from self-will and toward service and connection. Every day we choose to follow this path, we find that our old ways of fear and resentment lose their power. The Promises on pages 83-84 aren't just for newcomers—they renew themselves daily as we keep walking in this new direction.
7-5.discussion: What is one area of your life today where you can let go of your own plan and ask for a new direction from your Higher Power?

7-6.thought: Ah, my friend, fear is the great undertow that pulls us back toward the bottle. In the Big Book, we learn to identify it—not to shame ourselves, but to face it honestly. On pages 67-68, we're told to write down our fears: 'We reviewed our fears thoroughly.' This is the heart of the Fourth Step inventory. Once named, fear loses its power. And remember page 85: 'We are not cured of alcoholism. What we really have is a daily reprieve contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition.' That reprieve depends on spotting fear early and turning it over. So identifying fear isn't just a task—it's the first step toward the freedom described on page 84: 'We have entered the world of the Spirit.'
7-6.discussion: What is one fear you identified today, and how did you handle it—by holding onto it or letting it go?

7-7.thought: Letting go is the heart of our recovery. The Big Book teaches that our lives had become unmanageable because we tried to control everything ourselves. On page 60, it says, 'We were trying to run the show ourselves,' and that leads to misery. Letting go means turning our will and our lives over to God as we understand Him—a daily decision, not a one-time event. The Third Step Prayer on page 63 is a perfect example: 'God, I offer myself to Thee—to build with me and to do with me as Thou wilt.' That's releasing the illusion of control. And then we see the Promises on pages 83-84: we will experience freedom, peace, and a new sense of belonging once we truly let go. It's not about giving up; it's about trusting that a Higher Power can do for us what we could not do for ourselves.
7-7.discussion: What is one thing today that you are still trying to control, and how might letting go of it bring you closer to the freedom described in the Promises?

7-8.thought: The theme 'An Ever-Growing Freedom' speaks to the core of our recovery. In the Big Book, the Promises tell us we'll 'know a new freedom and a new happiness' [Page 83]. But notice: it says 'new'—not 'full' or 'final.' That's because freedom in AA is a living thing, expanding as we grow. The Promises unfold as we work the Steps: first freedom from the drink, then freedom from resentment, fear, and self-will. Each Step peels back another layer of bondage. Later, we 'cease to fight anything or anyone' [Page 84]—that's real freedom, not just from alcohol, but from the compulsion to control life. And the kicker? This freedom is never complete. It deepens as we continue to practice these principles in all our affairs, day by day.
7-8.discussion: Where in your life today do you still feel stuck, and how might turning that over to your Higher Power open a door to another layer of freedom?

7-9.thought: Ah, what a beautiful theme. To be an instrument is to surrender the illusion that we are the source of our own recovery. In the Third Step Prayer, we ask to be 'used'—to be of 'maximum service to God and the people about me' [Page 63]. This is the heart of Step 12: we don't create the healing; we become the conduit for it. When we work with another alcoholic, we are not the doctor, but the scalpel. The Seventh Step Prayer deepens this: 'Relieve me of the bondage of self, that I may better do Thy will' [Page 76]. If I'm still wrapped up in my own ego—my resentments, my fears—I'm a dull, useless tool. Being an instrument means daily maintenance: a moment of prayer in the morning to say, 'Use me today, however You see fit.' And at night, I check—did I let Him use me, or did I get in the way? The Promises tell us we will 'know a new freedom and a new happiness' [Page 83] when we become willing to be used for something larger than ourselves.
7-9.discussion: In what area of your life today are you most tempted to be the 'instrument maker' instead of the 'instrument'—to try to control outcomes rather than simply be available for use?

7-10.thought: Peace and serenity aren't prizes for a perfect life—they're the natural result of practicing the Twelve Steps daily. On pages 83-84, the Promises tell us we will 'know a new freedom and a new happiness' and 'feel the peace of God through the steps we have taken.' That peace isn't the absence of trouble; it's a deep confidence that we are no longer running the show alone. When we truly surrender our will and our lives to God's care (page 63, Third Step Prayer), we begin to experience 'a quiet and peaceful existence'—not because the world stops being chaotic, but because our response to it changes. Step 11 (pages 86-87) deepens this, teaching us through prayer and meditation to 'feel the presence of our Creator,' which brings the serenity to face any situation. In recovery, peace is a byproduct of trust—trust that as we stay spiritually fit, all things will work out for the best.
7-10.discussion: Where in your life today do you most need to trade your own will for trust in God, so that peace and serenity can take root?

7-11.thought: A turning point in recovery is that moment when we finally admit defeat and surrender to a Higher Power. The Big Book describes this as hitting bottom—when we realize that our alcoholic thinking is utterly bankrupt. On page 30, it says, "We were in a position where life was becoming very difficult, and we had but one alternative." That alternative is complete surrender. The Third Step Prayer on page 63 marks a profound turning point: we abandon ourselves to God, asking for release from our selfishness. And then, on pages 83-84, the Promises become real—we experience a new freedom, a new happiness, and a sense of serenity. That is the turning point: from captivity to freedom, from despair to hope.
7-11.book_ref: Chapter 3, pages 30-31; Chapter 5, page 63; Chapter 6, pages 83-84
7-11.discussion: What was the specific turning point in your own recovery that made you willing to try a different way of living?

7-12.thought: Giving up center stage means stepping out of the driver's seat of our own ego and letting a Higher Power take charge. The Big Book tells us that 'selfishness—self-centeredness! That, we think, is the root of our troubles' [Page 62]. When we insist on being the star of our own show, we miss the peace that comes from serving others. The Promises say 'self-seeking will slip away' [Page 84], which happens naturally when we focus on carrying the message to the still-suffering alcoholic rather than our own desires. Chapter 7 shows us the way: 'Practical experience shows that nothing will so much insure immunity from drinking as intensive work with other alcoholics' [Page 89]. By giving up the spotlight, we find lasting sobriety.
7-12.discussion: In what areas of your life are you still trying to be the director, and how might you practice giving up center stage today?

7-13.thought: Humility as a gift—that's a beautiful way to put it, isn't it? In the Big Book, humility isn't about groveling or thinking less of yourself. It's the honest admission that I am not the center of the universe, and that I need help from a Power greater than myself. On page 76, the Seventh Step Prayer asks God to 'remove my shortcomings'—that's a humble act. The Third Step Prayer on page 63 says, 'God, I offer myself to Thee,' surrendering our will and lives. That's humility in action. And here's the real gift: when we practice humility, we get a daily reprieve from our alcoholism. Page 85 says we are not cured but 'have a daily reprieve from this disease,' contingent on our spiritual condition—including humility. This gift keeps us sober and opens the door to peace.
7-13.discussion: Where in your life today can you practice the gift of humility by honestly admitting you need help?

7-14.thought: In recovery, we discover that the real nourishment isn't found in a bottle—it's in the spiritual principles we practice daily. The Big Book describes this as a 'new freedom and a new happiness' that comes from working the Steps [Page 83]. Just as food feeds the body, these principles feed the soul. The Promises tell us we will 'know a new freedom and a new happiness' and 'we will not regret the past nor wish to shut the door on it' [Page 83-84]. That's the nourishing ingredient: the honest practice of Step 10 and 11, which keeps us connected to a Power greater than ourselves.
7-14.discussion: What spiritual practice has been the most nourishing for your recovery today—prayer, step work, or helping another alcoholic?

7-15.thought: Pride, my friend, is the great enemy of recovery. The Big Book tells us that 'self-will run riot' is at the core of our disease [Page 62]. Pride convinces us we are the masters of our fate, that we can handle alcohol on our own, that we don't need help. But the first step humbles us — we admit we are powerless, that our lives have become unmanageable [Page 59]. The Seventh Step prayer asks to be relieved of 'the bondage of self' [Page 76], and when we work those steps, the Promises come true: 'We will lose interest in selfish things and gain interest in our fellows. Self-seeking will slip away' [Page 84]. Pride melts when we realize we are part of a greater whole, when we carry the message to the next suffering alcoholic.
7-15.discussion: Where does pride show up in your recovery today, and what step helps you set it aside?

7-16.thought: Humility in the Big Book isn't about thinking less of yourself—it's about realizing you're not the center of the universe. As Bill wrote, 'We admitted we were powerless'—that's the starting point [Page 59]. Step 7 puts it beautifully: 'Humbly asked Him to remove our shortcomings' [Page 76]. For me, a measure of humility means I can stop trying to run my own life and instead let a Higher Power guide me. It's a daily reprieve from the ego that kept me drinking [Page 85]. That's the kind of humility that keeps us sober—not groveling, just open.
7-16.discussion: Where in your life today do you need to let go of control and practice 'a measure of humility'?

7-17.thought: Surrender isn't weakness—it's the foundation for everything that follows. The Big Book tells us that the first step is to admit we are powerless over alcohol, that our lives had become unmanageable [Page 59]. This surrender opens the door to self-examination, because once we stop fighting, we can look at ourselves honestly. In Chapter 5, we're told to 'search out the flaws in our make-up' and be 'fearless and thorough' in that inventory [Page 65]. Without surrender, self-examination just becomes another way to blame or defend—but with surrender, it becomes the path to freedom. The Promises on pages 83-84 show that this combined work leads to a new freedom and a new happiness.
7-17.discussion: How does surrender open the door to honest self-examination?

7-18.thought: Gratitude is the foundation of a sober life. The Big Book promises that as we work the Steps, we 'will not regret the past nor wish to shut the door on it' [Page 83] — not because the past was good, but because we can see how it led us to recovery. This gift of perspective is something we receive, not earn. On page 85, it says: 'We will see that our new attitude toward liquor has been given us without any thought or effort on our part. It just comes!' That miracle deserves thanks. Gratitude for what we have — a daily reprieve, a new way of living, a fellowship of support — keeps us humble and willing to carry the message.
7-18.discussion: When was the last time you paused to thank your Higher Power simply for being sober today, with no strings attached?

7-19.thought: False pride is a subtle enemy in recovery, often masquerading as self-sufficiency. Bill W. himself wrote, 'I had a certain false pride' [Page 12] that kept him from admitting his true condition. In Step 12 work, the Big Book warns that when a prospect avoids us, 'Your own false pride may be touched' [Page 93] — and that's a signal to examine our motives. True humility, the opposite of false pride, is the foundation of each Step. The Seventh Step prayer asks God to remove 'selfishness, dishonesty, resentment, and fear' [Page 76]; false pride feeds all of these. Letting go of false pride means we can ask for help, share our defects without shame, and accept that we are not the center of the universe — a daily reprieve depends on this surrender.
7-19.discussion: When has false pride prevented you from asking for help or admitting a wrong? What would change if you set that pride aside today?

7-20.thought: This theme points straight to Step 7, where we humbly ask God to remove our shortcomings [Page 76]. It's not about self-improvement or willpower — it's about surrender. The Big Book says we 'cease fighting anything or anyone' [Page 84] and that God does for us what we cannot do for ourselves. Shortcomings are removed gradually as we practice Steps 10 and 11 daily [Pages 86-87]. The Promises assure us that 'we will not regret the past nor wish to shut the door on it' [Page 83] — that's the fruit of having our shortcomings lifted, not by our effort, but by a Power greater than ourselves.
7-20.discussion: What shortcoming have you been trying to remove on your own that you could humbly ask God to take from you today?

7-21.thought: In recovery, we often speak of the 'priceless gift' — and the Big Book makes clear that gift is not just sobriety, but a whole new way of living. On page 83, we read the Promises: 'We are going to know a new freedom and a new happiness.' That freedom and happiness are the priceless gifts that come from working the Steps. [Page 83] But perhaps the most profound gift is the ability to carry this message to others. As it says on page 89, 'Practical experience shows that nothing will so much insure immunity from drinking as intensive work with other alcoholics.' [Page 89] That is the gift that keeps on giving — we receive by giving it away. So the priceless gift is both the freedom we find inside and the privilege of passing it on.
7-21.discussion: What is the most priceless gift you have received from working the program, and how have you tried to share it with others?

7-22.thought: For someone in recovery, 'the good and the bad' means learning to accept life on life's terms, without the buffer of alcohol. The Big Book teaches that we can no longer run from our problems—we must face both the pleasant and painful moments with equanimity. On page 85, it says we have a 'daily reprieve' from alcoholism, but this reprieve depends on our spiritual condition, which requires us to accept both the joys and sorrows of each day. The Promises on pages 83-84 assure us that we will 'not regret the past nor wish to shut the door on it'—meaning even the bad experiences have value in our recovery. The key is to stop judging every event as 'good' or 'bad' and instead see each as a lesson or an opportunity for growth. As page 68 says, 'We asked God to help us show them the same tolerance, pity, and patience that we would cheerfully give a sick friend.' This includes ourselves—we must be patient with our own imperfections and the ups and downs of daily life.
7-22.discussion: Think about the last 'bad' thing that happened to you this week. How did your old thinking label it as bad, and how might the Big Book's perspective on acceptance change your reaction?

7-23.thought: When we say "I ask God to decide," we're practicing the heart of Step 3: making a decision to turn our will and our lives over to the care of God as we understand Him. This isn't a one-time event – it's a daily surrender. On page 63, the Third Step Prayer says, "God, I offer myself to Thee – to build with me and to do with me as Thou wilt." That's the essence of letting go and letting a Higher Power lead. Then Step 11 (pages 86-87) teaches us to "pray only for knowledge of His will for us and the power to carry that out." So asking God to decide means quieting our own frantic planning and saying, "Your will, not mine." It's the opposite of the self-will that ran riot in our drinking days. This practice, done morning by morning, gives us a daily reprieve from self-centered fear and opens the door to real peace.
7-23.discussion: What might change in your day if, before every decision, you paused and asked, 'What would a loving Higher Power have me do?'

7-24.thought: Helping others is not just a suggestion — it's the keystone that locks our recovery into place. The Big Book promises that when we work with another alcoholic, we receive a daily reprieve contingent on our spiritual condition [Page 85]. This isn't charity; it's survival. The book says, 'Practical experience shows that nothing will so much insure immunity from drinking as intensive work with other alcoholics' [Page 89]. So when we reach out to a still-suffering drunk, we're actually giving ourselves the best possible defense against that first drink. It's the practical application of Step Twelve, and it's where the promises come alive: 'We will suddenly realize that God is doing for us what we could not do for ourselves' [Page 83].
7-24.discussion: Think of someone you helped recently — did you notice any shift in your own sobriety or peace of mind afterward? What does that tell you about the connection between giving away what you've received and keeping it yourself?

7-25.thought: It means our sobriety is tied to helping others. As the Big Book says, 'Practical experience shows that nothing will so much insure immunity from drinking as intensive work with other alcoholics' [Page 89]. We didn't get sober alone, and we can't stay sober alone. The promises tell us 'We will carry the message to other alcoholics' [Page 84] — not as an option, but as a natural outcome of recovery. When I focus on those who still suffer, my own problems shrink and I stay connected to the real purpose of this program.
7-25.discussion: Is there one alcoholic I know who is still hurting, and what small step can I take today to reach out to them?

7-26.thought: Sobriety's worth isn't measured in days—it's found in the freedom from the obsession to drink, and in the new life that unfolds. The Big Book promises that when we sincerely follow the Steps, 'we will not regret the past nor wish to shut the door on it' [Page 83]. That's the real worth: our past becomes a teacher, not a tormentor. We gain a new sense of purpose, and even our worst mistakes are redeemed as part of our story. As it says, 'We will know a new freedom and a new happiness' [Page 83]. That's the priceless gift of working the program—not just staying dry, but living fully. Every sober day is a testament to the miracle of recovery, and it's worth more than any amount we ever spent on alcohol.
7-26.discussion: What would it mean for you to truly believe that your sober life is worth more than anything you ever got from drinking?

7-27.thought: Giving freely is the heartbeat of Step 12. The Big Book teaches that we have a debt to pay — not out of obligation, but because our own recovery depends on it. On page 77, it says "love and tolerance is our code," and that's what free giving looks like in action. When we share our experience, strength, and hope with a still-suffering alcoholic, we ask nothing in return. No payment, no gratitude, no guarantee they'll listen. We just give. And in that giving, we receive the daily reprieve [Page 85]. The Promises [Page 83-84] come true when we stop holding back: we intuitively know how to handle situations, we lose interest in selfish things, and we gain a new freedom. That freedom starts with a hand extended without strings attached.
7-27.discussion: What is one thing — a kind word, your time, or your story — you can freely give to another alcoholic or suffering person today, without expecting anything in return?

7-28.thought: In the Big Book, 'those who still suffer' is the heart of Step 12. On page 89, we read that 'nothing will so much insure immunity from drinking as intensive work with other alcoholics.' This means our very sobriety depends on carrying the message to the person still trapped in the nightmare. It’s not optional—it’s how we keep what we have. The book also says 'you can help when no one else can' [Page 151], because you’ve been there. So this theme reminds us that recovery isn’t just about us; it’s about being a channel of hope for the next sufferer. Every time we share our story, read the Big Book with a newcomer, or simply show up, we fulfill our purpose and strengthen our own sobriety.
7-28.discussion: Who is one still-suffering alcoholic you can reach out to today—with a call, a visit, or by sharing your experience?

7-29.thought: The Big Book whispers that true giving asks nothing in return. When we practice anonymous kindness, we echo the very heart of Step Twelve — carrying the message without needing our name on it. On page 89, it says: 'Practical experience shows that nothing will so much insure immunity from drinking as intensive work with other alcoholics.' That work isn't about recognition; it's about being a channel. On page 77, we learn that 'we lose our fear of today, tomorrow or the hereafter' when we give freely. An anonymous gift of kindness is a quiet, sacred thing — it wraps the giver in the promises of pages 83-84, where 'self-seeking will slip away.' So go ahead: do something kind today, and let it be a secret between you and your Higher Power. That's where freedom lives.
7-29.discussion: What is one anonymous act of kindness you can do today that no one will ever trace back to you?

7-30.thought: Ah, 'giving back'—or as we say in the rooms, carrying the message. The Big Book makes clear that our own recovery is never complete until we share it with others. On page 89, it says: 'You can help when no one else can. You can secure their confidence when others fail.' That's the heart of giving back: using our own wreckage and redemption to reach the still-suffering alcoholic. And it's not just noble—it's essential. On page 85 we read, 'Our real purpose is to fit ourselves to be of maximum service to God and the people about us.' Service keeps us sober. The promises on pages 83-84 come true not by sitting on our hands, but by 'working with others.' In fact, the book practically commands it: 'Above all, we should try to carry this message to alcoholics' (page 14). Giving back isn't an afterthought; it's the engine of lasting sobriety.
7-30.discussion: How has giving back—whether through sponsorship, service, or simply listening—strengthened your own recovery this week?

7-31.thought: Ah, my friend, prayer in recovery isn't just for the stormy seasons—it's for every season, every day. The Big Book teaches us that we 'pray only for knowledge of His will for us and the power to carry that out' [Page 76]. That's a prayer for all seasons because no matter what comes—joy, grief, temptation, or gratitude—we can turn our will over. The Third Step Prayer on [Page 63] isn't a one-time thing; it's a daily surrender. And the promises on [Pages 83-84] come to those who pray and practice these principles. So whether you're feeling on top of the world or at the bottom again, there's a prayer that fits. Keep it simple: ask for guidance, then get out of your own way.
7-31.discussion: What season of recovery are you in right now, and how can a simple prayer of surrender help you through it?

8-1.thought: Living it means that recovery isn't a theory you read about—it's a life you practice. The Big Book says, 'We sit in the silence of the library and try to absorb truth; but we dare not act upon it' [Page 85]. That's the danger: we can study the Steps, attend meetings, and still not live the program. "Living it" is the moment you pick up the phone to help another alcoholic—that's where the healing happens. The Promises on pages 83-84 come true 'only if we are painstaking about this phase of our development.' That phrase is key: painstaking. It means careful, persistent, daily action. Not a one-time fix, but a way of walking through life with the principles woven into every decision. And it's not grim—there's joy. We 'suddenly realize that God is doing for us what we could not do for ourselves' [Page 84]. Living it is the adventure of letting that happen one day at a time.
8-1.discussion: What is one area of your recovery where you've been 'sitting in the library' instead of 'living the book'—and what small action could you take today to change that?

8-2.thought: For someone in recovery, 'we become willing' reflects the heart of Steps Six and Seven—the quiet pivot from fighting our defects to letting them go. As the Big Book says, 'We asked Him to remove our shortcomings' [Page 76], but before that prayer comes a deep readiness. Willingness isn't about perfect surrender; it's about opening the door just a crack. The Promises follow: 'We will not regret the past nor wish to shut the door on it' [Page 84]. That freedom begins here, in the gentle act of becoming willing.
8-2.discussion: What small defect am I still holding onto because I'm not yet fully willing to let it go?

8-3.thought: To be of service is the heartbeat of recovery. Bill writes that 'practical experience shows that nothing will so much insure immunity from drinking as intensive work with other alcoholics' [Page 89]. This isn't just a nice idea—it's how we stay sober. When you carry the message to the still-suffering alcoholic, you're not just helping them; you're saving yourself. The Big Book promises that if you 'give freely of what you find and join us, we shall be with you' [Page 164], that you'll know a new freedom and happiness [Page 83]. Service is the key that unlocks the 12th Step and keeps your own recovery fresh. It doesn't have to be grand—a phone call, a chair at a meeting, a cup of coffee with a newcomer—but it must be genuine.
8-3.discussion: What small act of service could you do today to stay connected to your sobriety?

8-4.thought: Faith in this program often starts as nothing more than a tiny seed — a willingness to believe when you don't yet believe. In the chapter 'We Agnostics', we read that many of us 'had to believe in a Power greater than ourselves — that we could find a way out of our difficulties' [Page 47]. That willingness is the seed. We plant it by showing up, by listening, by trying the Steps even when we feel nothing. The Big Book promises that 'as we go through the day, we pause, when agitated or doubtful, and ask for the right thought or action' [Page 87]. That daily practice waters the seed. Before long, faith grows from a desperate hope into a quiet certainty — not because we reasoned our way there, but because we lived our way there. One day we realize we haven't doubted in weeks. That's the harvest.
8-4.discussion: What is one small act of faith you took early in your recovery that seemed insignificant then but now you see as a seed?

8-5.thought: Listening deeply means turning down the volume of our own restless thinking and tuning in — to the still, small voice within. The Big Book tells us that after our morning meditation, we ask for inspiration, an intuitive thought, or a decision [Page 86]. This isn't about perfecting our prayer technique; it's about quieting ourselves enough to hear a guidance that isn't our own. It’s a practice of surrender, repeated daily. And when we listen deeply to another alcoholic sharing their struggle, we hear our own story — and the solution we carry together. That’s where the miracle of Step Twelve starts: one ear, one heart, open.
8-5.discussion: When you sit in meditation or listen to another alcoholic, what do you notice inside yourself that tries to drown out the quiet voice of guidance?

8-6.thought: Ah, 'driven' — a word that captures the relentless engine inside the alcoholic. The Big Book describes this as a 'physical allergy' combined with a 'mental obsession' that compels us to drink even when we know it will destroy us. On page xxviii, the Doctor's Opinion states: 'These manifestations may be the direct outcome of the allergy of the body to alcohol.' But it's more than that — it's the 'strange mental blank spots' on page 42 that drive us back to the bottle against all reason. Recovery begins when we admit that this drive is stronger than our willpower. Step One [Page 59] asks us to accept that we are 'powerless over alcohol' — that the driver's seat is no longer ours. The program replaces that destructive drive with a new one: the desire to stay sober and help others. As page 84-85 promises, we are given a 'daily reprieve' from this compulsion, contingent on our spiritual condition. So when you feel that old drive stirring, remember it's not weakness — it's the disease talking. And you have a solution.
8-6.book_ref: Chapter 3, pages 30-43; Doctor's Opinion, pages xxv-xxxii
8-6.discussion: Think of a time when you felt 'driven' to drink or act out — what was the thought or feeling that seemed to take over? How did the Steps help you see that drive differently?

8-7.thought: The phrase 'A Design for Living' captures the essence of what the Big Book offers: not just a way to stop drinking, but a complete spiritual blueprint for a new life. On page 60, we read, 'We have found a basic design for living that works' — it's a simple, practical program built on the Twelve Steps. This design replaces the alcoholic's chaotic self-will with a God-centered life of honesty, service, and love. It's not a theory; it's a proven path that has restored millions to sanity and usefulness [Page 60, 163]. In living this design, we find that the Promises on pages 83-84 become real: we know a new freedom and happiness, and we intuitively know how to handle situations that used to baffle us.
8-7.book_ref: Chapter 5 (How It Works), pages 58-60, and Chapter 11 (A Vision For You), page 163
8-7.discussion: What specific change in your daily routine would better align you with the 'design for living' described in the Big Book?

8-8.thought: When we hear 'MADE A LIST . . .', we're talking about the Fourth Step inventory—the foundation of our recovery [Page 64]. This isn't just a to-do list; it's a fearless moral inventory of our resentments, fears, and harms done to others. On pages 64-65, we're told to list people, institutions, or principles we resent, and why. This process shines a light on the self-centered fear that drove our drinking. It's not about shame—it's about freedom. Once we see our part clearly, we can let go and move into Steps Five through Nine. That list is the key that unlocks the door to a new way of living.
8-8.discussion: What resentment on your list are you still holding onto today, and how might releasing it change your recovery?

8-9.theme: ". . . OF ALL PERSONS WE HAD HARMED"
8-9.thought:
Ah, my friend, you've touched on one of the most liberating, yet initially terrifying, parts of our journey. When we come to Step Eight, we read: 'Made a list of all persons we had harmed, and became willing to make amends to them all' [Page 76]. This isn't about shame—it's about freedom. The Big Book says we 'have a list of all persons we have harmed and to whom we are willing to make amends' [Page 76]. 

Notice it says 'all persons'—not just the ones we like, not just the ones who hurt us back. This is a full inventory of our wreckage. But here's the secret: the willingness itself is the spiritual experience. Page 77 says we begin to feel 'a new freedom and a new happiness.' By facing who we've hurt, we drop the heavy load of resentment and guilt. And when we actually make amends in Step Nine, we clean up our side of the street, and the promises come true: 'We will not regret the past nor wish to shut the door on it' [Page 83]. So that phrase, 'of all persons we had harmed,' is really an invitation to unburden your heart and walk free.
8-9.discussion: Is there a person on your list you've been avoiding? What would it feel like to become willing to make amends to them today, even if you haven't yet taken the action?

8-10.thought: Redoubling our efforts is not about trying harder in the same old ways—it's about remembering that recovery is a daily reprieve, not a permanent cure. As the Big Book says, 'We are not cured of alcoholism. What we really have is a daily reprieve contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition' [Page 85]. That maintenance takes work: prayer, inventory, amends, and carrying the message to others. When we coast, we drift. When we double down on the very actions that got us sober—especially the 10th, 11th, and 12th Steps—we renew our connection to the Power that keeps us sober. This isn't about grim effort; it's about joyful, persistent action. The Promises tell us we will 'not regret the past nor wish to shut the door on it' [Page 83], but only if we keep walking through that door every day. So redouble your efforts with a light heart—the Program meets you where you are, but it won't leave you there.
8-10.discussion: What one spiritual discipline—prayer, inventory, or service—have I let slip, and how can I renew it today?

8-11.thought: In the Big Book, 'ground glass' is Bill's vivid image for the destructive power of resentment. He writes that harboring resentment is like 'eating something that you know is poison' — it grinds away at your insides and your sobriety [Page 66]. The only way to remove it is through the searching and fearless moral inventory of Step 4, where we write down resentments and see our own part in them [Page 67]. Then, in Steps 5-7, we ask God to remove these defects, and we begin to live free of that grinding bitterness. For the recovered alcoholic, this daily removal is not optional — it's a lifesaver, because a single old resentment can still cost you your sobriety if you let it fester [Page 85].
8-11.discussion: What is one resentment you're still holding onto today that you haven't fully brought into the light of Step 4?

8-12.thought: Looking backward is not about wallowing in regret—it's about seeing the distance we've traveled. The Big Book promises that 'we will not regret the past nor wish to shut the door on it' [Page 83]. That backward glance shows us the pit we crawled out of, and reminds us that our drinking days were a nightmare of self-will and insanity. Yet, when we look back with sober eyes, we see how each stumble led us to this moment of grace. As it says, 'We will see that our new attitude toward liquor has been given us without any thought or effort on our part. It just comes!' [Page 84]. The past becomes a teacher, not a jailer. So when the Daily Reflection invites you to take a look backward, do it with gratitude—you're not the person you used to be, and that's worth celebrating.
8-12.discussion: What is one memory from your drinking days that you now see as a turning point rather than a failure?

8-13.thought: "A CLEAN SWEEP" calls us to thoroughly clear out the wreckage of our past, not leaving any hidden corner untouched. On [Page 64-65], the Big Book guides us to list and analyze our resentments, fears, and harms—to see them clearly so we can let them go. This isn't a half-hearted tidying; it's a deep purge of the old ways that kept us drinking.
8-13.discussion: What resentment or fear have you been avoiding sweeping out of your life, and what would it feel like to finally let it go?

8-14.thought: Repairing the damage isn’t about erasing the past—it’s about cleaning up the wreckage so you can walk forward without tripping over it again. The Big Book says, 'Though you may have to work with those you have injured, you will usually find that they are apt to be much more forgiving than you expect' [Page 80]. This isn’t guilt-tripping; it’s freedom. Step Nine clears the way for the new life you’re building. And here’s the beautiful part: 'We will not regret the past nor wish to shut the door on it' [Page 83]. That promise comes true when you’ve done the work. Repairing damage turns old shrapnel into stepping stones.
8-14.discussion: Is there one amends you’ve been putting off because you’re afraid of how it will be received? What’s the cost of continuing to carry that weight?

8-15.thought: Ah, the old 'didn't we hurt anybody' dance — one of our finest self-deceptions. In the Big Book, we read that the alcoholic 'is seldom sincerely trying to stop drinking' [Page 30] and that 'the great fact is that we were powerless over alcohol' [Page 30]. This theme cuts to the core of Step 1: admitting our drinking was not a private affair. The Promises assure us that 'we will not regret the past nor wish to shut the door on it' [Page 83], but only after we've faced the damage we caused. Those relationships we swore were fine? The book says we must 'clean up the past' [Page 76]. So this reflection asks us to drop the denial and see the wreckage we left behind — not to shame us, but to free us.
8-15.discussion: Who is one person you told yourself you didn't hurt with your drinking, but you now suspect was deeply affected?

8-16.thought: Ah, 'I had dropped out.' This phrase captures a feeling many of us know well—the sense of being utterly disconnected, not just from people but from life itself. The Big Book describes this in Chapter 3: 'We were in a state of being different from our fellows' [Page 30]. We felt like we didn't belong, that we had somehow missed the bus of normal existence. But here's the good news: dropping out is a symptom, not a sentence. The solution is found in the Steps, particularly Step Three, where we 'made a decision to turn our will and our lives over to the care of God as we understood Him' [Page 59]. This decision pulls us back in. And when we work the program, the Promises tell us we 'will suddenly realize that God is doing for us what we could not do for ourselves' [Page 84]. No more dropping out—we're finally part of the human race.
8-16.book_ref: Chapter 3, pages 30-32; Chapter 5, page 59; Chapter 6, pages 83-85
8-16.discussion: What does it mean for you to feel like you have 'dropped out' of life, and how has the program helped you reconnect with others and with yourself?

8-17.thought: Righting the harm is the heart of Step Nine—we make direct amends to those we've wronged, but it's not just about apologies. The Big Book says, 'We made direct amends to such people wherever possible, except when to do so would injure them or others' [Page 59]. This means we must be thoughtful, not reckless. Sometimes the bravest amends is staying silent to protect someone else. As Bill writes, 'We will not regret the past nor wish to shut the door on it' [Page 83]—amends free us from guilt and open the door to a new way of living. For those still resentful, the book counsels: 'Continue to watch for selfishness, dishonesty, resentment, and fear' [Page 84]. Righting harm is a daily practice, not a one-time event. It's the foundation of living free.
8-17.discussion: Is there a harm you've been avoiding making right because you're afraid of how it will be received? What would it cost you to try?

8-18.thought: Getting well, my friend, is not merely about putting down the drink—it's about a complete transformation of mind and spirit. The Big Book tells us that we have 'a disease which only a spiritual experience will conquer' [Page 44]. This healing begins when we admit our powerlessness and come to believe that a Power greater than ourselves could restore us to sanity [Page 59]. The Promises on pages 83-84 describe what getting well looks like: 'We will know a new freedom and a new happiness. We will not regret the past nor wish to shut the door on it.' That's the real wellness—not just sobriety, but a life of purpose and connection.
8-18.discussion: What does 'getting well' mean to you beyond just not drinking? Have you experienced any of the Promises in your own recovery?

8-19.thought: A frame of reference, in the Big Book's sense, is the new lens we get when we stop trying to run the show. Before the Steps, our only reference point was ourselves — our fears, resentments, and ego. But as we work Steps 1 through 3, we begin to see life from a spiritual perspective. The book promises that we will 'know a new freedom and a new happiness' [Page 83]. That shift in viewpoint is our frame of reference — instead of asking 'what do I want?' we start asking 'what is God's will for me?' [Page 85]. This new outlook makes even the toughest situations bearable, because we're no longer the center of the universe. As it says, 'We will see that our new attitude toward liquor has been given us without any thought or effort on our part' [Page 84]. That's the new frame of reference: a quiet confidence that a Higher Power is handling things.
8-19.discussion: Can you think of a time when your old frame of reference — your own will or fear — led you into trouble? How might a spiritual frame of reference change that situation today?

8-20.thought: Emotional freedom in recovery means releasing the bondage of self—those resentments, fears, and self-pity that once drove us to drink. The Big Book promises that we will 'know a new freedom and a new happiness' [Page 83] when we thoroughly follow the Steps. This freedom isn't about feeling good all the time; it's about being able to experience anger, sadness, or disappointment without being consumed by them. As we work Steps Four and Five, we let go of grievances that block us from emotional peace [Page 64-67]. And through daily Step Eleven, we ask for the right attitude, gaining 'the calm assurance of a full and useful life' [Page 87]. Emotional freedom is the quiet strength to respond rather than react—a gift of the program that grows with practice.
8-20.discussion: What resentment or fear can I release today to move closer to the emotional freedom the Promises describe?

8-21.thought: For many of us, the obsession with perfection kept us drinking. We had to be right, to be in control, to do things flawlessly. But in AA, we learn a different way: we just try. As the Big Book says, 'We are not saints. The point is, that we are willing to grow along spiritual lines' [Page 60]. That willingness—not flawless execution—is the key. Each day, we simply try to do the next right thing, to be honest, to help another alcoholic. The Promises remind us that 'We will suddenly realize that God is doing for us what we could not do for ourselves' [Pages 83-84]. Trying without demanding perfection opens the door to that grace.
8-21.book_ref: Chapter 5: How It Works, page 60; Chapter 6: Into Action, pages 83-85
8-21.discussion: What would it look like for you to release the pressure of 'getting it right' and simply 'try' today in your recovery?

8-22.thought:
Ah, seeking emotional stability—that's a theme that runs deep through every page of our Big Book, isn't it? In recovery, we find that stability isn't about a perfect, unruffled life; it's about a growing peace that comes from living in God's will. The Promises on [Page 83-84] tell us we will 'know a new freedom and a new happiness' and that 'the feeling of uselessness and self-pity will disappear.' That's the bedrock of emotional stability—not the absence of problems, but the presence of a new way of reacting to them.

Our program gives us practical tools for this. The daily reprieve [Page 85] reminds us that our recovery—and our emotional balance—depends on 'our vital relationship with God.' That means staying close to our Higher Power through prayer and meditation [Page 86-87], constantly turning over our will. And when we feel shaky, we can revisit the Seventh Step prayer [Page 76], asking to be 'relieved of the bondage of self,' which is usually the root of our emotional turmoil.

So stability isn't a destination; it's a daily action. It's the result of working Steps Ten and Eleven consistently [Page 84-88], continuing to take personal inventory and promptly admitting when we're wrong. That keeps our side of the street clean and our hearts steady.
8-22.discussion: What specific situation or feeling today makes you want to cling to your own will instead of trusting your Higher Power for stability?

8-23.thought: Bringing the message home means living the principles of recovery within your own family. It's easy to be a saint at an AA meeting, but the real test is at the dinner table. The Big Book reminds us that 'we have no scruples about asking you to remake your family relationships' [Page 133] and that 'the family is the proving ground of our new way of life.' [Page 134] We must practice tolerance, honesty, and forgiveness not just with other alcoholics, but with our spouses, children, and parents. This is where the 12 Steps truly come alive. If we can carry the spirit of Step 12 into our own homes, we discover that the Promises aren't just for the meeting hall—they're for the kitchen, the living room, and the bedroom too. The message isn't something we export; it's something we embody where we live.
8-23.discussion: What is one specific way I can bring the message of recovery into my home today, especially in a relationship that has been strained by my drinking?

8-24.thought: The phrase 'A RIDDLE THAT WORKS' captures the beautiful paradox at the heart of our recovery. We come to AA convinced that we must control our drinking, yet the first step asks us to admit we are powerless [Page 59]. That seems like nonsense—how can surrender solve anything? But the Big Book teaches that 'half measures availed us nothing' [Page 25]; we had to go all in on a spiritual solution that defies logic. Then the Promises come true: 'We will suddenly realize that God is doing for us what we could not do for ourselves' [Page 84]. The riddle is that by giving up our will, we find freedom; by giving away what we've received, we keep it. This program works not because it makes sense to the ego, but because it aligns us with a Power greater than ourselves.
8-24.discussion: Where in your own recovery have you experienced something that seemed like a riddle—a step or principle that didn't make sense at first but ended up working beautifully?

8-25.thought: Bonding is not just a nice feeling—it is the very fabric of recovery. When we connect with another alcoholic, we are practicing Step Twelve, and the Big Book promises that 'we will lose interest in selfish things and gain interest in our fellows' [Page 84]. This gift of bonding happens most powerfully when we share our experience, strength, and hope with someone who still suffers. Bill's own story shows how one conversation with Dr. Bob sparked a chain reaction that saved millions [Page 13]. In Chapter 7, we are told that 'life will take on new meaning' when we become part of this web of mutual rescue [Page 89]. Bonding is the practical expression of love and service that keeps us sober. It is not about perfection—it is about showing up for another alcoholic and letting them show up for you.
8-25.discussion: When have you felt the deepest sense of bonding with another alcoholic in recovery? What made that connection possible?

8-26.thought:
Your instinct is right — 'Giving It Away' points straight to Step 12. The Big Book teaches that the price of our sobriety is giving it away. On [Page 89], it says, 'Practical experience shows that nothing will so much insure immunity from drinking as intensive work with other alcoholics.' That's not a suggestion — it's a survival principle. The Promises on [Page 84] also hint at this: 'We will suddenly realize that God is doing for us what we could not do for ourselves.' But that realization only stays alive when we share it. Giving it away is actually how we keep it; the message grows stronger every time we pass it along.

I've seen this in my own life: when I hold onto my recovery like a secret, it starts to mildew. But when I share my story, read the book with a newcomer, or just listen, my own sobriety gets a fresh shot of life. The Big Book calls this 'carrying the message' — not lecturing or saving, just sharing what was freely given to us. And the miracle is, the more we give, the more we receive. That's the paradox at the heart of our recovery.
8-26.discussion: Who is one still-suffering alcoholic you can reach out to this week — not to fix them, but just to share what helped you?

8-27.thought: CENTERING OUR THOUGHTS. In the Big Book, this means turning our frantic, self-willed minds toward a Power greater than ourselves. When we try to run our own show, our thoughts spin out of control — resentment, fear, self-pity. But as Bill writes, 'We asked God to direct our thinking... and we ceased to fight anything or anyone' [Page 86]. This centering is not a one-time event; it's the daily discipline of Step 11: 'conscious contact' through prayer and meditation [Page 85]. The promises tell us 'we will intuitively know how to handle situations which used to baffle us' — that's what happens when our thoughts are centered, not scattered [Page 84].
8-27.discussion: What thought pattern keeps pulling you off center, and what specific action can you take today to gently bring it back toward your Higher Power?

8-28.thought: Ah, my friend, 'lightening the burden' — this is the very heart of our recovery. When we carry the message to the still-suffering alcoholic, we lift not only their load but our own. The Big Book tells us on page 89: 'Helping others is the foundation stone of your recovery.' As we practice the Twelfth Step, we find that 'the burden of our past is lifted' [Page 83] and we are given a daily reprieve contingent on our spiritual condition. The Promises assure us that 'we will not regret the past nor wish to shut the door on it' [Page 84]. Carrying the message is not a duty — it is a privilege that frees us from self-obsession. When we share our experience, strength, and hope, we lighten our own burden by giving away what we have so freely received.
8-28.book_ref: Chapter 7: Working With Others, pages 89-103; also Chapter 6: Into Action, pages 83-85
8-28.discussion: Think of a time you shared your recovery story with another alcoholic. How did carrying that message lighten your burden that day?

8-29.thought: Choosing anonymity is a profound spiritual decision, not a mere preference for privacy. The Twelfth Tradition tells us that 'Anonymity is the spiritual foundation of all our Traditions, ever reminding us to place principles before personalities' [Page 565]. In recovery, this means we let go of ego and self-seeking. When we carry the message to still-suffering alcoholics, we do so not for personal recognition but because 'Practical experience shows that nothing will so much insure immunity from drinking as intensive work with other alcoholics' [Page 89]. Anonymity protects our singleness of purpose—it keeps the focus on the message, not the messenger. By choosing anonymity, we practice humility and ensure that the Fellowship remains a place where any alcoholic can find help without the distractions of status or fame. It is a daily discipline of putting our recovery and the group's unity above our own desire for credit or attention.
8-29.book_ref: Chapter 7 (Working With Others) and the Twelve Traditions, pages 89-103 and 563-566
8-29.discussion: Think about a time when you wanted to receive praise for your recovery work. How did remembering the principle of anonymity help you refocus on the true purpose of helping others?

8-30.thought: Friend, the phrase 'The only requirement...' points to one of AA's most radical and beautiful principles—Tradition Three. The Big Book states plainly: 'The only requirement for A.A. membership is a desire to stop drinking' [Page 564]. That’s it. No dues, no fees, no moral or religious tests, no social standing. It means every alcoholic who walks through the door is welcome, exactly as they are. The program of recovery asks for honesty, open-mindedness, and willingness [Page 58], but the *membership* itself has just that one simple condition. So when you feel like you don’t measure up or that you’re not ‘good enough,’ remember: the only requirement is a desire to stop. That desire is already inside you. Come as you are. You belong.
8-30.discussion: What would change in your recovery if you fully accepted that the only requirement is a desire to stop drinking—nothing more, nothing less?

8-31.thought: The Big Book makes clear that our program is unique because it offers a daily reprieve from a seemingly hopeless condition — not a cure, but a spiritual solution that works one day at a time [Page 85]. Unlike medical or moral approaches that try to fix the alcoholic, this program addresses the underlying spiritual malady: self-will run riot [Page 62]. It is unique because it requires no money, no education, only willingness: 'Rarely have we seen a person fail who has thoroughly followed our path' [Page 58]. The Steps are suggestions, not commands, yet they lead to a profound transformation that no other method has consistently achieved [Pages 59-60]. What makes it truly singular is that the therapy is carried by one alcoholic helping another, without professional direction [Page 89].
8-31.discussion: What has surprised you most about how the AA program differs from other attempts you've made to find peace or sobriety?

9-1.thought:
Willingness to grow is the heartbeat of recovery. In the Big Book, we read that 'we must be entirely ready to have God remove all these defects of character' [Page 76]. That readiness isn't passive—it's an active, daily choice to say "I'm willing to let go of fear, resentment, and self-will, and let something new grow in their place." Step 6 and 7 are really about this: we can't force change, but we can cultivate the willingness that invites it.

Growth in AA isn't about becoming perfect; it's about becoming whole. The Promises remind us that 'we will intuitively know how to handle situations which used to baffle us' [Page 84]. That kind of wisdom comes from practice, from making mistakes and getting back up. But it starts with a simple prayer: 'Take away my difficulties, that victory over them may bear witness...' [Page 76]. Willingness to grow means trusting the process, even when we can't see the outcome.

So what does this look like today? Maybe it's asking for help when you'd rather pretend you're fine. Maybe it's reading the Big Book with an open mind instead of a critical one. Willingness is a muscle—the more you use it, the stronger it gets. And it's never too late to start flexing.
9-1.discussion: What is one area of your life today where you feel resistance to change—and what would it look like to say 'I'm willing to grow' in that area, even if you don't know how?

9-2.thought: Finding a reason to believe is the quiet turning point where despair meets hope.
